newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Belgian musicians' collective out to Zap the world.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Belgian musicians' collective out to Zap the world.

text.p: How many famous Belgians can you name?...Eddy Merckxx? Rene Magritte? Hercule Poirot? Tin-Tin? Jacques Brel? Adolphe Sax? Plastic Bertrand?

You're getting closer with the last three because Zap Mama, a Brussels-based voice and rhythm group led by acappella diva Marie Daulne, plans to be the next big-time music export from the land which spawned the saxophone and Django Reinhardt.

Daulne, daughter of a Belgian father and a Zairean mother, is setting out on a world tour with her seven-piece group, taking her blend of Euro-African voice-based music to the United States, Europe, Japan, Australia and maybe back to Africa.
And for her there is a distinct message that Zap Mama can take to the world a balance between nature and technology that can bring peace and well-being to a turbulent world.

"We have lost a lot from nature. Sounds from nature have a lot to offer, to satisfy and to calm. We need nature. That's why we lose ourselves and become crazy in the western world," she said in an interview before the Amsterdam concert of her tour.

"People need drugs to get away from pressures in the western world. If you go to nature, to the desert, to the forest you can feel good. Being outside with oxygen can give you the feeling. You really don't need anything else," she said.
Daulne says she is at the front of current trends, offering the world the sounds it wants without the electronic culture and drugs that go with it.
"I don't like plastic. I like the real thing. I do trance music. African music is very trance, it's like techno but with real sounds," she said.
Daulne started the first Zap Mama incarnation in the late 1980s, winning attention and acclaim with her five-voice female acappella group.
But why Zap? and why Mama?

"Easy," says Daulne, looking faintly surprised at the question. "Zap is what changes all the time, it's changes in music. Mama is because I play with the sounds from Mother Earth, the sounds of nature."
"I use the noises we have around us, sometimes it's a buzz from insects or whatever, and I'm trying to put harmony on that," she said.
The new Zap Mama is moving on, adding percussion and an electric bass as well as traditional African instruments and a male voice, but the fascination with harmony remains.
It's a mix which can be powerful, as she showed at a sound check, blending French and English lyrics in a sweeping ballad before giving way to a thundering bass-and-drum reggae beat.
BAND A MULTI-RACIAL MIX

Her current band is a mix of a Dane, two Belgians, an Amsterdammer, a Londoner, a Jamaican and a native of the Ivory Coast, all living in Belgium and all working towards Daulne's vision of what Zap is, and should, be.

The avante-garde music world is also fascinated by Zap music. Daulne has worked closely with David Byrne, frontman of cult New York rockers Talking Heads and synthesiser pioneer Brian Eno. She has spotted Herbie Hancock, Bobbie MacFerrin and Chakka Kahn at her concerts.

Hancock and MacFerrin, both well-known for experimenting with voice techniques, are clearly drawn by Daulne's theories about music and the human voice, theories which bring constant invitations to teach jazz workshops around the world.
"In the evolution of music, all instrument techniques are very far advanced but the voice is not very far," says Daulne.
"With the saxophone, for instance, you do a lot with the airflow, but voices just stop. We've had scat but not really a big evolution. I see a lot of different ways to sing from my culture."
Being of mixed race gives her unique insight, she said.

"I balance the influences perfectly. I take them both. If I had only the African culture I wouldn't have arrived at what I do because the organisation of Europe and technology have helped me a lot. I can have money, go in planes and travel where I want. The Belgian side is good for me, it gives me freedom in the modern world."
It is a freedom she has used to the full, gathering for instance, Taureg sounds after living with a tribe in Mali.

"Sometimes I'll hear something and think "what's that?" I'll try the sound, to do it you can't just listen, you have to see how they do it. You also have to see how they live, where these sounds come from."
For Daulne, as she and her band criss-cross the globe attracting the avant garde vanguard, the music comes first with a political message not very far behind.

"I want to get through to the western audience. Before I wanted to talk to Africans. But now I want to open something up here in Europe. Don't forget we're not alone. Try to take care of the others who are human like you," she said.
